attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own essay, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: The firm 'will' is kept, and so is the antecedent 'once the money stops flowing'. The source's 'because' clause gives the causal reason; it is not a separate condition. No deadline is stated.

contract.note: Reading the antecedent as a broad drying-up of investment, not one market drop, is a fair, ordinary reading. The speaker gave no threshold for money stopping, so whether the antecedent has occurred depends on that interpretation.

evidence.note: Reuters (Oct 19, 2026) reports OpenAI and Anthropic are still actively raising capital. That cuts against the antecedent having occurred, but it says nothing about whether improvements stopped.
Reports a fall in Chinese AI share prices. Falling stock prices do not show that funding for LLM development has stopped, and the item has no evidence about capability.

reviews.rationale: This is a conditional forecast with no deadline. The packet does not show the antecedent happening: Reuters reports active fundraising, and the Chinese stock decline is not a broad funding stop. Its status is unknown, so the forecast cannot be scored, and there is no post-condition capability evidence either way.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own essay.

semantics.note: Keeps all three parts as written, including 'literally only good for AI'. The phrase 'no post-Dot Com story' leans rhetorical, but treating it as part of a present-state claim is reasonable.

contract.note: Defining mass-market as an established, substantial commercial market, and separating technical capability from real demand, is an ordinary reading. The result depends on how 'mass-market' and 'good for' are read, since the speaker set no size threshold.

evidence.note: A 2022 NVIDIA disclosure about H100 support for scientific computing. It predates the target period, is the company describing itself, and does not measure non-AI demand.
The NSCC allocation policy, effective July 2026, spreads H100 and H200 time across research categories, but it does not separate non-AI use or show a mass market.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows that AI GPUs can technically run scientific workloads and that a national supercomputer shares GPUs across research uses. Neither item measures substantial commercial non-AI demand in August 2026, or how AI facilities are reused. The evidence neither establishes nor refutes the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words. The scare quotes read as emphasis or self-quotation, not as quoting another person.

semantics.note: Keeps the universal 'literally anyone involved'. The claim is close to hyperbole, but it is firm and unhedged.

contract.note: Because the speaker wrote 'literally anyone', one credible net-positive case contradicting the claim is a fair reading. 'Economic sense' has no stated measure, and the contract has to tie the benefit to improved capability.

evidence.note: A 2025 randomized trial found no significant overall time saving. Its savings figure is a projection, not a realized net benefit, and it does not isolate gains from model improvement.

reviews.rationale: The only evidence item reports projected, not realized, savings and no significant overall time reduction. It neither proves the universal negative nor gives a credible case of realized net benefit from improved capability. The packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion. He names no source for the figures.

semantics.note: Mostly faithful. The source says the labs are 'allowing them to burn' tokens, while the normalised text says users are 'burning' them. The contract correctly treats this as permitted allowance.

contract.note: Valuing allowances at API prices and testing a July majority is a fair reading. I disagree with the contract's flag of false: its own ambiguity flags (allowance vs use, API value vs serving cost, free users, which population) could each change the result.

evidence.note: A June 2026 secondary report on SemiAnalysis's tests of maximum allowances. Wrong month, and it has no user-weighted distribution showing what a majority received.
A secondary summary: one test per plan run to its limit gave up to about 40x on Claude Max and 70x on ChatGPT Pro. These are top-tier plan capacities, not what most users get.

reviews.rationale: The evidence covers only the maximum allowances of individual top-tier plans in June 2026. One sits inside the $20–40 range and one above it. There is no representative July distribution showing what most users were allowed, so the majority claim cannot be confirmed or refuted.
